title: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima (1945)
hookLine: a Jesuit with medical training cares for the wounded after the atomic bomb
carry: he turned the house into a hospital

lines: A JESUIT HOUSE ON THE HILLS.
A FLASH, THE WINDOWS BLOW IN.
THE WOUNDED WALK UP THE ROAD.
cards: A Spanish priest is in his room in a Jesuit house on the hills outside Hiroshima, where he trains young men who want to become Jesuits.

Before joining the order he had studied medicine, though he hadn't practiced as a doctor in years. Then a blinding flash, a roar, and the windows blow in. He and the others climb the hill and look toward the city.
It is burning. Before long, the wounded begin walking out of the smoke and up the road toward them. His name is Pedro Arrupe, and today, a damaged house and some half-forgotten training.

teach.b: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. In his own later account, the house was cracked and battered but still standing. So he and the young Jesuits turned it into a hospital.
The chapel, the rooms, the halls filled with people lying on mats. There was almost no medicine.
He writes of doing what little he could with what was on hand, cleaning burns, trying to understand injuries no medical school had ever taught him.
The young men became nurses overnight. They went into the ruins looking for survivors, and fed people from whatever food they could find. Arrupe didn't claim to have been a hero.
What he describes is mostly helplessness, and staying anyway.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WEEK, IN ONE HOUSE.

teach.b: God in all things, even in a city in flames. Contemplatives in action: a house of prayer that became, without a vote, a house of nursing. Cura personalis, one burned person at a time.
The magis, which in that moment simply meant: open the door wider. And after yesterday's teaching that cost something, here is care that costs something.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus names the people he will recognize at the end, and among them, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me." Arrupe later led the whole Society of Jesus.
But the story people still tell is this house on the hill, and a man doing the next small thing because he was the one who was there.

how: Catholics pray for the victims of war and for peace at Mass and in private prayer, and Arrupe's account of caring for the wounded at Hiroshima is often retold in Jesuit schools and retreats.

games.q: what does “pedro arrupe at hiroshima” mean?
o: a Jesuit who turned his damaged house into a hospital
a Jesuit doctor sent to Japan to run a city clinic
a priest who blessed the city before the bomb fell

games.q: Arrupe at Hiroshima — tap the pairs.

s: Arrupe was a practicing doctor in Hiroshima
he had studied medicine before joining the Jesuits, but had not practiced in years.
the Jesuit house was badly damaged but still standing
so it became a hospital for the wounded.
Arrupe described himself as a hero
his account is mostly about helplessness, and staying anyway.

games.q: you're Pedro Arrupe. the city below is burning, your house is cracked, you have almost no medicine, and the wounded are walking up the road. what do you do?
o: leave for somewhere safer and better supplied.
turn the house into a hospital and do what little you can.
wait for proper doctors to arrive.
games.why: he and the young Jesuits turned the house into a hospital. his own account dwells on how little he could do, and that they stayed.

practice: Picture the road up the hill and the people walking out of the smoke, then think of one place at war right now: the people there whose names you'll never know, and those caring for them with almost nothing.
Don't picture the worst; give them your breathing, one breath at a time. If you pray, pray for them and for peace; if you don't, let them stay in your thoughts a while.

wordCard.voice: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. A Jesuit with old medical training who turned a damaged house of prayer into a hospital for the wounded. Today's word, and the end of this week.

carryVoice: Your line: he turned the house into a hospital. Helplessness, and staying anyway. That closes the week.
